extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, and critics (especially American poets/writers seeking a national poetic identity)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for poets and literary makers to create a native American poetry: candid, democratic, emotionally free, engaged with modern science and history, avoiding mere imitation of English models and salon-parlor prettiness. Includes prescriptions on subject matter (national history, sex, nature), tone (candor, character), and aesthetic aims (stimulate reader, suggest rather than over-define).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom as prerequisite for great poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: We first require that individuals and communities shall be free; then surely comes a time when it is requisite that they shall not be too free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom (political and social) is the foundational condition from which a native national poetry can grow; the social conditions of liberty are treated as prerequisites to the emergence of a great, indigenous poetic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere imitation of English tone and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: American poets have 'caught the English tone and air and mood only too faithfully' and are often indistinguishable from English poets in diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write as if you were on the Thames when you are on the Hudson; strive for authentic national diction and thought rather than reproducing imported forms. Anti-pattern: poems that read as English pastiches or prize-man/anthology-pleasing verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free expression of emotion; arouse and initiate
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetry of the future aims at the free expression of emotion... and to arouse and initiate, more than to define or finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize energetic, inciting emotional expression over polished, fully-resolved statements. Poems should open possibilities and prompt response rather than provide exhaustive definitions or closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulate reader's imagination; suggest rather than explain
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest poet is he who in his works most stimulates the reader's imagination and reflection... he, not all of whose meaning is at first obvious, and who leaves you much to desire, to explain, to study, much to complete in your turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write so the reader is invited to participate mentally and imaginatively. Avoid over-explication and finished completeness that leaves no work for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character over style or polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Character, a feature far above style or polish--a feature not absent at any time, but now first brought to the fore--gives predominant stamp to advancing poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize moral/psychic depth and distinctive voice rather than technical virtuosity or elegant surfacecraft. Anti-pattern: technically perfect but hollow or socially irrelevant verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry akin to outside life and landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more akin, likewise, to outside life and landscape... real sun and gale, and woods and shores--to the elements themselves--not sitting at ease in parlor or library listening to a good tale of them, told in good rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground verse in lived, physical environments and elemental experiences rather than insulated salon scenes. Use concrete natural particulars to connect to broader democratic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject fractional/select surface melody in favor of the sturdy and universal
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevailing flow of poetry... has been an expression of mere surface melody, within narrow limits... Above all things it is fractional and select. It shrinks with aversion from the sturdy, the universal, and the democratic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing narrowly decorative or superficially musical poems that refuse broad or democratic themes. Aim for robustness and universality in subject and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with science and modern principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Science, having extirpated the old stock-fables and superstitions, is clearing a field for verse... with the new principles behind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate contemporary scientific understandings and the modern intellectual climate; see science as enlarging poetic possibilities rather than as inimical. Use modern ideas to supply fresh themes and eliminations of outdated superstitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patriotism and national history as worthy grand subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Never had real bard a task more fit... to sing worthily the songs these States have already indicated... to express the native forms, situations, scenes... the great problems of man and freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take large national subjects—origins, founding, major wars, geography, social fusion—as material for epic or sustained poetic treatment. Avoid trivial domestic motifs when the national scale is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as representative of democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In the highest walks of art it [democracy] has not yet had a single representative worthy of it... the United States most need... a central, spinal reality of native-born teachers, artists, littérateurs...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce work that embodies democratic ideals and speaks to the broad population (farmers, mechanics, common people), not exclusively elite tastes. Poetry should arise from and be answerable to democratic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glorifying past violence or feudal splendor
rubrics_metrics.description: Not the satin and patchouly of today, not the glorification of the butcheries and wars of the past, nor any fight between Deity on one side and somebody else on the other--not Milton, not even Shakspere's plays, grand as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not romanticize or aestheticize historic barbarities or feudal grandeur as ends in themselves. Seek new modes and classes of poetic subjectivity appropriate to modern democratic times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on interior (microcosm) and Man rather than exterior macrocosm
rubrics_metrics.description: Still, the rule and demesne of poetry will always be not the exterior, but interior; not the macrocosm, but microcosm; not Nature, but Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While using natural and national scenes, center the poem on inner human experience, consciousness, moral life, and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance gratitude to foreign influences with humility and adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meantime, we can (perhaps) do no better than to saturate ourselves with, and continue to give imitations, yet awhile, of the esthetic models... Let the sources be enlarged... remembering that at present, and doubtless long ahead, a certain humility would well become us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and draw from foreign literatures (British, Spanish, French, German, Scandinavian, Oriental) but adapt and transform them into work adjusted to American realities rather than merely copying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candid, physiological treatment of sexual themes in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The sexual passion in itself, while normal and unperverted, is inherently legitimate, creditable, not necessarily an improper theme for poet... the assumption of the sanity of birth, Nature and humanity, is the key to any true theory of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sexuality frankly and scientifically in literature to combat repression and social disease; candidness is defended as ethical and aesthetic. Anti-pattern: euphemistic, furtive, or prudish avoidance that fosters ignorance and morbidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confront taboos ethically for social and artistic health
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventional... has led to states of ignorance, repressal, and cover'd over disease and depletion... The time seems to me to have arrived... for a new departure--a third point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an ethic of candor and scientific temper when addressing taboo subjects; doing so is both an artistic duty and a public-health–oriented act that supports wider social progress (including women's eligibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should aid social progress (e.g., women's rights) by sensible treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: To the movement for the eligibility and entrance of women... the current prurient, conventional treatment of sex is the main formidable obstacle... There will in my opinion be no general progress... till a sensible, philosophic, democratic method is substituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literature's treatment of sexual and social themes to remove obstacles to political and social reform; avoid exploitative or prurient representations that set back reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of the nude in art with ethical purpose and trained execution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary for the future of English art and of English morality that the right of the nude to a place in our galleries should be boldly asserted; it must, however, be the nude as represented by thoroughly trained artists, and with a pure and noble ethic purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representing the nude, do so from informed anatomical and aesthetic study and with a moral/educational aim, not to stimulate base passions. Anti-pattern: crude, exploitative nudes or use of nudity for titillation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough familiarity with the human form to judge beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The human form, male and female, is the type and standard of all beauty of form and proportion, and it is necessary to be thoroughly familiar with it in order safely to judge of all beauty which consists of form and proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists and writers should study anatomy and the ideal human form so as to recognize and promote healthy standards; this knowledge prevents harmful fashions (e.g., tight-lacing) and distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'beauty disease'—don’t let taste for beauty override truth and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The immoderate taste for beauty and art... leads men into monstrous excesses... There is a lust, a disease of the art faculties, which eats up the moral like a cancer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep aesthetic appreciation subordinated to moral truth; avoid allowing pursuit of beauty alone to corrode moral judgment and social health.
